transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Hi, first time buying. Not sure what I should look at first tbh.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: No worries—you don’t need to figure everything out at once. A good place to start is whether you’re buying to live in or as an investment, then what monthly payment feels comfortable and which areas work for you. Is this mainly for your own stay?

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Probably for my own stay, but not immediately—maybe in a year or two. I’m staying with my sibling for now, so still figuring out what makes sense.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: That makes sense—if you’re thinking a year or two ahead, there’s no need to rush. When you picture having your own place, what would matter most: having more space to yourself, being near a particular area, or keeping the monthly cost comfortable?

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Probably keeping the monthly cost comfortable first. I haven’t really settled on an area yet, and don’t want to stretch myself just to get a place.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: That’s sensible—better to set a comfortable monthly ceiling before narrowing down areas or homes. Do you have a rough monthly amount you’d feel okay with, without stretching? An estimate is fine.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Honestly, I haven’t worked out a number yet. I’m a bit worried about underestimating what I can afford, especially with the other costs on top of the monthly payment.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: That’s a sensible concern. Instead of starting with a property price or the maximum a bank might lend, it helps to work from your regular commitments, allow for one-off purchase costs and ongoing expenses like maintenance and utilities, then leave a buffer. No need to settle on a number today. Which feels less clear—the upfront costs or the ongoing costs?

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Probably the upfront costs—I’m not sure what I’d need to pay besides the deposit. The whole process feels a bit intimidating, so it’d help to know the main things to plan for first.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message:
That can feel like a lot at first, but you can plan it as a checklist. In Malaysia, besides the deposit, buyers commonly need to budget for the sale agreement and loan legal fees, stamp duties on the transfer and loan documents, and related searches, registration and other disbursements. For a subsale, there may also be a valuation fee; insurance or takaful costs depend on the financing and arrangements.

The exact amounts vary by property, loan and eligibility for any current relief. Some new-launch packages may cover certain costs, so get an itemised estimate and confirm what’s included before committing. It’s also worth keeping a separate buffer for moving, utilities and any furnishing or renovation. You don’t need to settle on a budget today—starting with this checklist is a good first step.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Thanks, that checklist makes it feel a bit less overwhelming. Would it make sense to work out a comfortable monthly budget first, then check what financing I might qualify for before viewing places?

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: Yes, that’s a sensible order. First work out a monthly amount that feels comfortable after your regular commitments, savings and a buffer for ownership costs. Then ask a bank or licensed mortgage adviser for an indicative financing check. Treat that as an estimate, not a spending target—the lender’s limit may be higher than what feels comfortable. It should give you a more grounded range before viewing, with no need to rush.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: That sounds manageable. For an indicative check, do I need a specific property in mind, or can I ask based on my income and commitments first? I’m not quite ready to make a formal application yet.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: It may be possible to get an initial indication without choosing a property, but requirements vary by lender or adviser. I’ll check what they’d need for a non-formal estimate based on your income and commitments. We can keep it to an information-gathering step for now—no need to apply yet.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Thanks, appreciate it. For a rough check, would they usually just need ballpark income and monthly commitments? I’d rather not send documents around before I’m ready.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: It may be possible to start with approximate figures, but I can’t confirm whether those alone are enough—requirements vary by lender or adviser. You can ask whether they’ll provide a no-document estimate before sharing anything. There’s no need to send documents before you’re ready.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Okay, that’d be helpful if you could check whether they offer a no-document estimate. I’m fine sharing rough income and monthly commitments, just not documents or a formal application yet.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: Understood—you’re comfortable sharing rough figures, but not documents or making a formal application. I can’t confirm yet whether a lender or licensed adviser offers a no-document estimate, so I’ll check whether that’s available and what ballpark details they’d need. No need to send anything or apply at this stage.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Thanks, that works. Please let me know what they say about a no-document estimate—I’ll stick to rough figures for now.
